title: {{NAME}} and the Silver Pitch of the Northern Queen
moral: The goal worth celebrating most is the one that cost you something to give away.

pages.content:
The Silver Pitch was a rumour before it was a destination. Players spoke of it in changing rooms the way people speak of things they have never seen but believe in absolutely: a football pitch in the far north where the grass grew silver instead of green, the goalposts were carved from white birch, and the game played there meant something beyond the match itself.

{{NAME}} had heard the rumour in four different cities and finally followed it to its source, which turned out to be a valley ringed by mountains so tall their peaks wore clouds like hats, and at the valley's floor, gleaming under a pearl-grey sky, exactly as described.

The Silver Pitch. Real. Enormous. And occupied.

Two teams were already warming up. One wore deep violet and silver, the Northkeep Royals, led by a girl whose crown was worked into her captain's armband rather than worn on her head, which {{NAME}} found practical and somehow very dignified. She was Princess Elara, and she moved on the pitch with the specific confidence of someone who has played here their whole life.

On the opposite touchline, enormous and serene, stood three unicorns in the silver grass, wearing matching violet training bibs with the patient readiness of players who have been through a warm-up before and know not to waste their energy on it.

A fourth figure stood beside them, holding a bag of match balls and watching {{NAME}} arrive.

'Referee is late,' this figure said. 'Can you do it?'

pages.content:
The figure holding the match balls was a boy named Aren, who served as the squad's manager, medic, water carrier, and occasional amateur referee, and who explained all of this with the cheerful efficiency of someone who enjoys being useful.

The visiting team, it emerged, was a unicorn squad. This was apparently a regular fixture. The Northkeep Royals played the Northern Herd twice per season in what Aren described as 'technically a friendly but not at all friendly in practice.'

'They're remarkable,' Aren said, nodding toward the unicorns who were taking shots at an empty goal with precision that made the word remarkable feel modest. 'Fast, excellent first touch, and they communicate telepathically, which means no calling for the ball, no shouting formations. They just know.'

{{NAME}} watched the lead unicorn, a grey-dappled stallion named, according to Aren, Fenn, take a free kick from distance with his right front hoof. The ball curved with absolute intention into the top corner.

'Can Elara's team win?' {{NAME}} asked.

Aren tilted his head. 'They always come close. Elara is the best footballer I've ever seen who isn't a unicorn. But in the last five games, in the last minutes, when it's level, she always passes to the wrong moment.' He paused. 'She tries to make the goal instead of take it. Like she needs it to be for someone else before she'll let herself.'

{{NAME}} considered this. He thought he understood it more than he could easily explain.

pages.content:
The match on the Silver Pitch was unlike any football {{NAME}} had refereed, which was, admittedly, none, but he was confident this would be unlike anything anyone had refereed.

The unicorn herd moved in patterns that were beautiful and baffling, always three steps ahead, always knowing where each other was without looking. Elara's team met them with organisation and heart, pressing hard, forcing the herd to work, and Elara herself was extraordinary, reading the game at a level that seemed almost like its own kind of telepathy.

She created two goals in the first half: one by finding a diagonal pass so angled and weighted that it seemed to bend time, and one by drawing two defenders and laying the ball off to her striker with such precise timing that the whole sequence looked rehearsed.

But Elara herself had not scored. Every time she had the chance, something happened. The pass instead. The lay-off. The redirect.

Fenn noticed. {{NAME}} could see it, the great grey head turning to Elara during play, tracking her specifically with a gaze that was more than tactical.

At halftime Fenn walked directly to Elara, which was unusual, as the unicorns usually kept their side at halftime. He stood before her and pressed his forehead very gently to hers, and the two of them were still for a moment, Elara's eyes closing.

She walked back onto the silver pitch standing differently. Not straighter. Stiller, somehow. Like she had put something down.

pages.content:
Ninety-second minute. Two goals apiece. Elara was through.

The unicorn keeper was out fast, cutting the angle, and Elara had the fraction of a second in which a decision lives and dies. {{NAME}} held his breath on the touchline.

She shot.

Not a pass. Not a lay-off. Not for anyone else. Hers.

The ball went low to the keeper's right, exactly where keepers least expect the ball from a right-footed player who has spent the whole match demonstrating she prefers her left. The keeper went the wrong way. The ball hit the back of the white birch net and the silver grass around the goal erupted, blades of it rising as if lifted by the sound of the stadium.

Elara stood still for one second with her arms at her sides, looking at the goal.

Then Fenn arrived. Not galloping. Simply there, the way things that are meant to happen find their moment without apparent effort. He lowered his head and touched his grey muzzle to Elara's shoulder, and she reached up and held onto his neck with both arms and pressed her face against his mane.

Aren was crying, he said, because of the altitude, which was not credible given the valley was very low, but {{NAME}} chose not to challenge it.

The Silver Pitch was very quiet. The kind of quiet that has been earned.

pages.content:
The post-match was gentle and full of company.

Both teams stayed on the silver grass as the pearl-grey sky deepened toward evening, talking and resting, and the unicorns proved to be excellent company once the match was done, nudging various players companionably and accepting scratches behind their horns with democratic enthusiasm.

Fenn found {{NAME}} sitting at the touchline and stood nearby, not especially close, not especially far, in the manner of a creature who has decided you are acceptable without requiring this to be a dramatic announcement.

{{NAME}} scratched behind Fenn's horn. Fenn permitted this.

Elara sat down beside {{NAME}} with a cup of something warm from Aren's flask. 'You're a good referee,' she said.

'I've never refereed before,' {{NAME}} said.

'I know,' she said. 'You watch people the right way. You watch them trying, not just what they're doing.'

He walked home in the long northern dusk, the Silver Pitch at his back, the mountains enormous and the stars beginning to find their places in the pale sky.

He slept quickly and deeply, and in the comfortable space between waking and sleep, he heard the particular percussion of hooves on silver grass and the sound of a ball striking the white birch frame of the goal and a voice that might have been Aren's, excited and specific.

'Come back for the second fixture,' it said. 'Fenn has been practising a new shot. Nobody's seen it yet. Except you'll want to.'
